sources.text:
I thank you, Mr. President, for convening this timely open debate, which provides a valuable opportunity to identify concrete ways to make the Council’s work more effective, transparent and representative. We are firmly convinced that a more functional Security Council is essential to strengthening multilateral cooperation and restoring public confidence in the United Nations.

In this regard, working methods, the vehicle through which the Council exercises its mandate, must continue to evolve in order to enhance the Council’s ability to fulfil its primary responsibilities.

The deep divisions among Council members have significantly hampered the Council’s ability to manage many of the pressing crises on its agenda, and in this context, working methods have sometimes been used to advance political objectives rather than to improve the Council’s transparency and effectiveness. Conversely, establishing informal understanding on recurring matters could allow members to save time and focus on substantive issues, improving the overall functioning of the Council.

Furthermore, the delay experienced this year in appointing Chairs of subsidiary bodies and penholders clearly pointed to the need to explore practical solutions to avert a similar impasse in the future. Last year’s note by the President of the Security Council on its working methods (S/2024/507) emphasizes that members with relevant expertise, regional perspectives, experience chairing subsidiary bodies and specific interests can add value as penholders. A clearer process could help the implementation of this commitment.

In this context, we underline the importance of ensuring that permanent and non-permanent members operate on as equal a footing as possible. We are convinced that the distribution of duties among the Council members should be fairer and more balanced in order to allow the elected 10 members of the Council to contribute even more. Moreover, it is essential that the views and interests of Member States concerned by any matter on the Council’s agenda be heard and taken into account in its work.

Looking ahead, the upcoming selection process for the next Secretary-General further underscores the need for inclusive and predictable working methods, in order to ensure transparency in this sensitive process.

Improving working methods must also be viewed in the wider context of a comprehensive and meaningful reform of the Security Council aimed at making it more transparent, democratic, efficient and more accountable to the broader membership. It is difficult to address working methods without recognizing at the same time the root causes of the Council’s recurrent paralysis, which are directly linked to the veto, regardless of whether it is actually used or simply threatened. For this reason, Italy supports all initiatives that seek to impose self-limitations on the use of veto, such as the French-Mexican initiative and the code of conduct of the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency Group, and proudly co-sponsored resolution 76/262 on the veto initiative. This is also one of the main reasons why we do not support the expansion of the category of permanent members, which would inevitably generate additional vetoes. Such an expansion would undermine the effectiveness of the Council, in addition to creating further discrimination and divisions among its members and reducing its inclusiveness and accountability.

Finally, to strengthen the authority of the Council, Italy reiterates the importance of fully applying Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter of the United Nations, according to which any member of the Council involved in a dispute, including the permanent members, should abstain from voting on decisions pertaining to that situation.

sources.text:
I thank the briefer for her insightful remarks.

Entrusted with the primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security, the Security Council acts on behalf of the wider membership and in the collective interest of the international community. Its working methods are, therefore, central to its legitimacy and credibility. Today, more than ever, ensuring the Council works collectively, efficiently and transparently, while maintaining the confidence of the membership it serves, is imperative. In this regard, allow me to make four points.

First, we must address the use of the veto and the risk of Council paralysis. While the Charter of the United Nations provides permanent members with a distinct voting prerogative, the exercise of the veto should not come at the expense of the Council’s ability to discharge its responsibilities. Malta, apart from being a member of the Uniting for Consensus group, continues to support initiatives aimed at promoting the responsible use of the veto, including the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency Group’s code of conduct, the Franco-Mexican initiative and the General Assembly veto initiative. Malta also reaffirms its support for efforts to ensure the full implementation of Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter, supporting a dedicated chapter in the Council’s annual report on its application.

Secondly, inclusivity must remain at the heart of the Council’s working methods. For the Council to act on behalf of the wider membership, its working methods must ensure meaningful opportunities for engagement beyond the Council itself, including with the General Assembly and with regional organizations, to strengthen its ability to respond to situations on its agenda. Inclusivity should also extend beyond the intergovernmental system. Civil society, affected communities and women and youth offer vital perspectives and lived experiences. Malta encourages the Council to make full use of interactive formats to ensure the meaningful and safe participation of briefers and other voices.

Thirdly, the Council must ensure the effective functioning of its subsidiary bodies. Malta remains concerned that Chairs and Vice-Chairs have yet to be appointed for the Council’s subsidiary bodies. These bodies perform an important role in supporting the Council’s work and the absence of agreed leadership impedes their ability to discharge their mandates effectively. We urge Council members to engage constructively and make an effort to reach agreement on these appointments without delay.

Fourthly, transparency and accountability must remain at the centre of the Council’s working methods. Transparency remains essential to build confidence in the Council and in the wider multilateral system. Of particular significance is the ongoing process for the selection and appointment of the next Secretary -General. The manner in which this process is conducted and the confidence it inspires among the wider membership will have implications well beyond the Council and for trust in the Organization as a whole. Malta calls for increased openness in the selection process and supports efforts aimed at providing the General Assembly with a meaningful choice in the appointment of the next Secretary-General.

Note by the President S/2004/507 provides an important framework for improving the Council’s working methods, but its value ultimately depends on its faithful and meaningful implementation. Malta stands ready to work constructively with all members in advancing these efforts and ensuring that the Council is equipped to respond effectively to the challenges before it.

sources.text:
I thank you, Mr. President, for convening this open debate. As this is the first time my delegation is taking the floor during your presidency, allow me to also wish you every success as you carry out your duties.

Spain reiterates its firm commitment to strengthening the working methods of the Security Council, convinced that a more representative, democratic and transparent Council is also a more effective body, better equipped to respond to the contemporary challenges to international peace and security. When procedures are inclusive and predictable, the legitimacy of the Council’s decisions is clearly strengthened.

Note by the President S/2024/507 represents a valuable exercise in consolidating good practice, which must continue to evolve in order to respond to the new challenges facing the Council.

Spain considers it a priority to strengthen those provisions designed to ensure more systematic interaction between the Council and the wider membership. To this end, it is essential to improve the predictability of the Council’s work and ensure timely acc ess to documentation and information, which are key to guaranteeing inclusiveness and the effective participation of Member States.

The Toledo formula, introduced by Spain in 2015 during our presidency of the Council, is a concrete example of how to move in this direction. Closing meetings are not merely a monthly summary, but a forum for dialogue that promotes transparency, interaction and accountability.

We also believe it is necessary to expand opportunities for dialogue and confidence-building through more frequent use of informal meetings and interactive discussions. It is also important to strengthen the practice of sharing draft texts well in advance and to promote more inclusive negotiation processes.

With regard to the application of rules 37 and 39, Spain attaches great importance to the participation of those States particularly affected by the issues under consideration by the Council. A consistent, predictable and transparent application of these r ules is essential, as the participation of those States provides valuable perspectives and information for the deliberations.

To facilitate broader consensus, it is essential to move towards a more balanced division of labour among the members of the Council, particularly with regard to the allocation of the drafting of resolutions.

Spain also supports the strengthening of cooperation between the Security Council and the General Assembly, in line with the resolution on the revitalization of the General Assembly, as well as the relationship with the Peacebuilding Commission.

Finally, we call for greater scrutiny of the use of the veto and for strengthened accountability. We urge, once again, all Member States to join the Franco-Mexican initiative, which promotes restricting the veto in cases of mass atrocities, and the Accountability, Coherency and Transparency Group’s Code of Conduct. We believe that both initiatives should be incorporated into the Council’s rules of procedure. We also recall that Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter of the United Nations applies to all members of the Council.

In conclusion, the Security Council’s working methods must be adapted to respond appropriately to contemporary realities. Our common objective must be to ensure that the provisions of presidential note 507 are translated into tangible practices and results that strengthen the legitimacy and effectiveness of the Security Council.

sources.text:
We appreciate this opportunity to discuss the working methods of the Security Council. The continued dialogue with the broader United Nations membership is key to ensuring the transparency, inclusiveness and cohesion of its work.

Lithuania believes that, in order to effectively fulfil its primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security, the Council must adapt its work to the changing international realities. Lithuania also shares the concerns expressed by other speakers regarding the continued delays in appointing Chairs of subsidiary bodies and their impact on the Council’s ability to fulfil its mandate. Moreover, with the ever-expanding scope of issues addressed by the Council, it is increasingly important to ensure that the voices of the broader membership are heard. In this regard, rule 37 of the Council’s provisional rules of procedure must be applied consistently, particularly when considering acts of aggression and mass atrocities. Rule 37 participants should also receive sufficient advance notice of the opening of the speakers’ list and timely confirmation of their inclusion in the list.

The use of the veto remains a critical concern. The use, or rather abuse, of the veto power by Russia to shield itself from accountability for its illegal aggression against Ukraine cannot be ignored. Lithuania remains a steadfast supporter of efforts to limit the use of the veto, particularly in situations of mass atrocity, genocide and war crimes. We encourage all delegations to commit to the Accountability Coherence and Transparency code of conduct and the French-Mexican initiative. The adoption of General Assembly resolution 76/262, establishing the veto initiative, marked a significant and long-overdue step. Lithuania also recalls that the veto power is constrained under Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter of the United Nations, which obliges a party to a dispute to abstain from voting. Further consideration should be given to ensuring full implementation of this key provision.

Lithuania joins calls for greater transparency in the Council’s deliberations, including through a better balance between public meetings and closed consultations and more meaningful interaction with the wider United Nations membership. The valuable contribution of civil society briefers must also continue to be protected and encouraged.

Improving working methods cannot replace comprehensive Security Council reform. However, practical procedural improvements need not wait for such reform. We urge the Council to heed these calls and translate this dialogue into concrete action.

sources.title: Mr. De Wolf (Belgium), speaking on behalf of the Benelux countries; Belgium: European States; Invited non-members of the Security Council; European Union member States; NATO members; High-income economy (World Bank, that year) — Security Council, 10210th meeting (resumption 1), 19 August 2026 — S/PV.10210 (Resumption 1) — Implementation of the note by the President of the Security Council (S/2024/507)

sources.text:
I have the honour to speak on behalf of the Benelux countries — a long-standing regional partnership comprising Luxembourg, the Kingdom of the Netherlands and my own country, Belgium.

At the outset, we thank the Danish presidency for having convened this open debate on the working methods of the Security Council. We also wish to sincerely thank the Executive Director of Security Council Report for her briefing and recommendations.

The Benelux countries firmly believe that improving the working methods of the Security Council is essential to strengthening its transparency, accountability, inclusiveness and effectiveness. At a time when the credibility of multilateral institutions is at stake, improving working methods is fundamental.

We would like to highlight four points.

First, we share the concerns voiced by many delegations regarding the current deadlock in the appointment of Chairs and Vice-Chairs of subsidiary bodies. A record delay has severely affected the work of the Council. Delays should not become the norm. We encourage Council members to identify practical solutions and contingency measures that will ensure the timely allocation of these responsibilities and the uninterrupted functioning of the Council’s subsidiary organs.

Secondly, the forthcoming appointment of the next Secretary-General is of critical importance for the United Nations. The Benelux countries continue to advocate for a fair, transparent and inclusive selection process, conducted on an equal basis for all candidates and fully in line with the relevant General Assembly resolutions and established good practices. We welcome the public hearings of candidates and improvement of the preliminary stages of the selection process. However, transparency could be enhanced, in particular if the Security Council could communicate the results of the straw polls it conducts. More broadly, we see clear merit in further strengthening the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly. Enhanced exchanges between these two organs can contribute to greater accountability, transparency and trust across the membership. The General Assembly’s role as the most representative body of the United Nations should be fully reflected in these efforts.

Thirdly, according to Article 24 of the Charter, the Security Council acts on behalf of the entire membership of the United Nations. Its working methods should therefore be as transparent and inclusive as possible. We encourage the continued use of mechanisms that facilitate meaningful exchanges with the wider membership, including Arria-formula meetings, direct interaction with stakeholders, non-governmental organizations and civil society representatives. These can enrich the Council’s understanding of ongoing crises. We also support strengthening interaction between the Security Council, the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council and the Peacebuilding Commission, as well as ensuring that the Council benefits from relevant expertise across the United Nations system, including from the human rights pillar.

Finally, the continued use and threat of use of the veto remain one of the principal obstacles to the Council’s ability to fulfil its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. The Benelux countries reiterate their supp ort for initiatives aimed at promoting restraint in the use of the veto, particularly in situations involving mass atrocities. We also welcome efforts by the General Assembly to enhance accountability following the use of a veto. We further recall the importance of Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter, which stipulates that a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. Respect for this provision would strengthen confidence in the impartiality and credibility of the Council.

The Benelux countries remain firmly committed to supporting improvements to the working methods of the Security Council. A more transparent, inclusive and effective Council is in the interest of all Member States and essential to the credibility of our multilateral system.

sources.text:
We thank Japan for convening this important debate. With increasing conflict around the world, the effective functioning of the Security Council has never been more crucial. We commend Japan’s leadership as Chair of the Informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions. We welcome an update to the note by the President S/2017/507, which must remain a living document and adapt to changing conditions.

Australia’s goal for working methods reform is to increase the Council’s effectiveness, transparency and accountability. To that end, we support the holding of open Council meetings whenever possible. We welcome open debates, which enable the broader membership to inform the Council’s work. We believe that the Council’s work benefits from hearing from diverse briefers. That includes regional and subregional organizations, non-governmental organizations and civil society. We reiterate our strong support for more civil society, especially women and humanitarian briefers and ask the Council to ensure their safe participation without reprisals. We welcome the greater democratization of penholder responsibilities, which are increasingly led or shared by elected members.

We support the Council’s increased coordination with other United Nations organs, including the Peacebuilding Commission, which is uniquely placed to support the Council’s work on conflict prevention and peacebuilding. With a high level of conflict around the world and a humanitarian system that is overstretched, we need to focus more on conflict prevention and sustainable peacebuilding.

The veto is an is a powerful instrument and its use must be transparent and restrained. We reiterate our strong support for all efforts to achieve that, including discussions on Article 27, paragraph 3, which stipulates that a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. We look forward to further constructive engagement with all Member States as we seek to shape a Security Council that can more effectively respond to the challenges of today.

I have the honour to speak on behalf of the Benelux countries: Belgium, the Kingdom of the Netherlands and my own country, Luxembourg. Although I will speak on behalf of three Member States, I will try to keep the remarks succinct. We align ourselves with the statement to be made by my colleague, the Permanent Representative of Switzerland, on behalf of the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency (ACT) Group.

We thank Sierra Leone for convening this open debate. We express our gratitude also to the Co-Chairs of the Informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions, Denmark and Pakistan, and to Ms. Loraine Sievers and Ms. Shamala Kandiah Thompson for their valuable inputs.

The Benelux countries believe that improving the working methods of the Security Council is key to fostering its transparency, accountability and effectiveness. We deeply regret that the Council often finds itself in a deadlock, which prevents it from fully executing its mandate. This failure to act often has devastating consequences for civilians affected by conflict.

The Benelux countries would like to make three points.

First, the use of the veto and the threat of use of the veto overshadow the Council’s working methods and are at the root of the Council’s paralysis. We therefore support initiatives to limit the use of the veto, such as the proposal made by France and Mexico, and the code of conduct developed by the ACT Group. We also believe that all members of the Council must adhere to Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter of the United Nations. We encourage adding new language in note by the President S/2024/507 on the inclusion of a dedicated section on the use of the veto in the Council’s annual report.

Secondly, the significant delay in appointing Chairs and Co-Chairs of subsidiary bodies of the Council for 2025 has had a negative impact on the work of the Council, including with regard to the protection of children in armed conflict and the implementation of the sanctions regimes established by the Council, which are of interest to the entire membership. We encourage Council members to find effective ways to ensure the timely appointment of Chairs of its subsidiary bodies in the future.

Thirdly, as we prepare for the selection and appointment of the next SecretaryGeneral, in 2026, we emphasize the importance of ensuring transparency and inclusivity throughout this process. It is essential that the process be conducted in full accordance with General Assembly resolution 79/327, building on the good practices established in 2015–2016. Enhancing transparency in the Council’s deliberations and reinforcing the role of the General Assembly are key.

The Benelux countries remain firmly committed to supporting the improvement of the working methods of the Security Council. It is in the interests of us all that the Council fulfil effectively its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security, acting on behalf of all of us.

sources.title: Mr. Pereira Sosa (Paraguay) (spoke in Spanish); Paraguay: States of the Americas; Invited non-members of the Security Council; Group of 77 members; Upper-middle-income economy (World Bank, that year) — Security Council, 10210th meeting (resumption 1), 19 August 2026 — S/PV.10210 (Resumption 1) — Implementation of the note by the President of the Security Council (S/2024/507) — English text is the UN's translation from Spanish

sources.text:
At the outset, Mr. President, we wish you every success in your presidency.

The delegation of the Republic of Paraguay appreciates the opportunity to take the floor in this debate and congratulates Denmark on its presidency of the Security Council. We consider the annual debates on the Council’s working methods particularly important for the development of an efficient and effective collegial body capable of fulfilling its mandate under the Charter of the United Nations. We also thank the Executive Director of Security Council Report for her briefing.

Given the Security Council’s responsibility for achieving and maintaining international peace and security, it has a duty to facilitate the implementation of the three pillars of the United Nations work. The Security Council is of fundamental importance in the United Nations system. Its work has an impact on other areas, including on the Economic and Social Council, the establishment and deployment of peacekeeping operations, the protection of human rights, the Peacebuilding Commission, the International Court of Justice and the General Assembly itself, as well as, more broadly, on the implementation of the peace architecture as a whole.

One of the first points to highlight is that the Council continues to operate under provisional rules of procedure. To achieve greater transparency, stability, predictability and legal certainty, it is necessary to update and adopt rules of procedure that meet formal and substantive requirements and enable the Council to function effectively.

Predictability in the appointment of chairs and vice-chairs of subsidiary bodies, the rotating presidency with pre-established safeguards to ensure that non-permanent members can exercise that function at least once during their terms of membership, and transparency in negotiations leading to resolutions, presidential statements and notes affecting the rules of procedure are all matters of great importance, given the Co uncil’s influence within the United Nations. The current procedural situation increases the power imbalance not only between permanent and non-permanent members, but also between Council members and the wider membership of our Organization.

The relationship between the General Assembly and the Security Council remains of paramount importance. Our delegation believes that this relationship must be strengthened and that the Council must recognize that its legitimacy depends on respect from the entire United Nations membership and on faithfully fulfilling its mandate. The Council must therefore strive to be more representative, inclusive, transparent, effective and accountable for its decisions.

The peace and security pillar is under the close scrutiny of the international community. Although the Security Council is not a body of universal representation, its work serves, to a large extent, as a global barometer of the performance of the United Nations in maintaining international peace and security. In that regard, we welcome the efforts of the Informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions to publish its annual report, guided by the principles of openness, dialogue and inclusion. This should continue.

Member States have witnessed significant divergences over the use of the veto during recent sessions of the intergovernmental negotiations on the reform of the Security Council. Paraguay believes that the veto should be formally abolished, limited or restricted, in particular in cases involving measures intended to prevent the most serious crimes or mass atrocities. Furthermore, it is vital to recognize that the exercise of this power must reflect the great responsibility it entails. The veto must therefore be used with full transparency and prudence, and its use carries a duty of accountability, in accordance with the principle of the sovereign equality of States set out in Article 2, paragraph 1, of the Charter. Likewise, we believe that Members of the Uni ted Nations cannot comply selectively with the Charter, and, accordingly, we call for full compliance with Article 27, paragraph 3.

The Council’s annual reports constitute an obligation with respect to the General Assembly as a whole. We believe that they should be less descriptive, more analytical, provide greater thematic depth and not omit analysis of the most sensitive decisions taken by the Council in a given year.

Finally, Paraguay advocates maximum transparency, inclusion and equity in the selection of the Secretary-General. We recognize the leading role of the Security Council in that process but consider it vitally important that the role of the General Assembly not be limited to simply endorsing the Council’s recommendation.

sources.heading: Security Council, 9571st meeting — Letter dated 1 March 2024 from the Permanent Representative of Japan to the United Nations addressed to the Secretary-General (S/2024/208/Rev.1)
sources.text:
I thank you very much, Mr. President, for convening this timely and important discussion. We commend Japan for taking up the important work of promoting transparency and accountability of the Council as Chair of the Informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions. We also thank the previous Chair of the Informal Working Group, Albania, for the good work done during the past two years. I also thank our briefer this morning, from Security Council Report, for her very insightful remarks.

We welcome the statement on working methods delivered earlier today by Mozambique on behalf of the 10 elected members of the Council (E10). We share the views of the E10 on this topic.

Please allow me to make some additional points in that connection.

First, it is important that we keep in mind that the Council’s working methods is fundamentally about ensuring transparency, which is essential for the credibility of the Security Council and for the multilateral system, as a whole. It is true that there has been an increase in the number of open Council meetings, and we welcome that development. Notwithstanding that positive trajectory, the trend, it seems, is still for some topics to be discussed in closed consultations only. We understand the need for closed discussions to facilitate frank exchanges among Council members. Nonetheless, it is important to keep in mind that the topics that are discussed in closed discussions are often of great concern to all Member States. We should therefore find a way to have their views incorporated and reflected in those discussions. We think that more effort should be made to convene some of those meetings in open format, allowing for the participation of concerned Member States. At the very least, if an open meeting is not possible, summary records of the closed consultations should be made available to the wider membership.

Secondly, the Council acts on behalf of the wider membership on international peace and security and should be accountable for its decisions. Singapore had previously suggested, pursuant to paragraph 129 of note by the President S/2017/507, that an exchange between the Council and the wider membership should take place when the annual report is being drafted. We are therefore very pleased that the United Kingdom has taken up that initiative. It convened an informal consultation on the annual report in January, and we hope that will become an annual practice going forward for future presidencies.

We also note that paragraph 138 of note 507 encourages the President of the Council in charge of presenting the report to the General Assembly to report to the Council members on relevant suggestions and observations raised during the General Assembly debate on the annual report. However, it is not clear to us if there has been any such reporting back to the Council members of the General Assembly debate. We would suggest that the Council members convene soon after the General Assembly debate to assess and discuss the General Assembly debate on the annual report of the Council. It is also important that a summary of that meeting of the Council be shared with all Members of the United Nations.

We also call on all Council Presidents to submit their monthly assessments pursuant to paragraph 136 of note 507, as those provide an important flow of information from the Council to the wider United Nations membership. In 2023, just 7 of 12 Council Presidents submitted their monthly assessments. There needs to be more concerted and genuine effort in that regard.

Thirdly, the effectiveness of the Council has taken a sharp dive in the past year. Just last week, we met in the General Assembly to discuss yet another veto which prevented the Security Council from issuing an urgently needed response to the conflict in Gaza. Since resolution 76/262 on the veto initiative was adopted in April 2022, we have seen 12 vetoes. That merits a deep reflection on the section on “Intra-Council Cooperation and Consultation” in note 507, including paragraphs 74 to 77. In particular, we think it is time to insert concrete ideas into the updated note, which Japan has indicated it will produce and which we welcome, in order to clearly articulate the United Nations membership’s expectation for Council members, in particular the permanent members, to act in unity to discharge their responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. Singapore also supports the FrenchMexican initiative and the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency group’s code of conduct on limiting the use of the veto against mass atrocity crimes. And we believe that Council members, in particular the permanent members, should abstain in the voting if they are a party to a dispute, in line with Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter of the United Nations. We believe that Article merits further discussion within the context of the Council.

I conclude by thanking Japan for its continued efforts on this issue and look forward to practical reforms under its leadership. Singapore supports your intention, Mr. President, to follow up on today’s debate through deliberations on an updated note 507. We call on all Council members, particularly the permanent members, to engage constructively in that initiative to improve the working methods of the Council.

sources.heading: Security Council, 10043rd meeting — Letter dated 6 November 2025 from the Permanent Representative of Sierra Leone to the United Nations addressed to the Secretary-General (S/2025/719)
sources.text:
I thank you very much, Mr. President, for convening this timely and important discussion. We commend the co-Chairs of the informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions, Denmark and Pakistan, for taking up the important work of promoting the transparency and accountability of the Council. I also thank the briefers from Security Council Report and Security Council Procedure for their insightful opening remarks. We welcome the statement on working methods of the 10 elected members of the Security Council, delivered earlier by the Ambassador of Pakistanl . We share their views on this issue and would like to offer some additional perspectives.

First, the Council’s working methods are fundamentally about ensuring transparency. Transparency is the foundation for a credible, effective and accountable Security Council. Transparency has a positive impact, not just on the work of the Council and the implementation of the Council’s decisions. It will also promote greater dialogue and transparency beyond the Council in the broader peace and security domain. In this regard, while we commend the increase in the number of open meetings of the Council, we continue to observe that closed consultations remain a regular practice for certain files. While we understand that closed discussions may be necessary for more candid exchanges among Council members, we think that more effort should be made to convene some of these meetings in an open format, allowing for the participation especially of concerned Member States. At a minimum, some form of summary record, at least on decision points, should be produced for closed meetings and shared with the wider membership.

Secondly, we want to see a more inclusive and consultative Council. We are encouraged that Council members have made greater use of formats such as Arria Formula meetings to engage with the General Assembly. We also appreciate the regular wrap-up meetings with the wider membership by the presidency for each month and hope that these will progress towards more interactive discussions and analyses, instead of being yet another occasion to deliver prepared statements. In this connection, the report of the Security Council to the General Assembly is important for the accountability of the Council towards the wider membership. For all Member States to have a considered debate on the work of the Council, these reports should be made available to members early. Singapore strongly supports the suggestion, in paragraph 148 of note by the President S/2024/507, for interactive informal exchanges of views with the wider membership when the annual report is being drafted. We also note that paragraph 157 of presidential note 507 encourages the President of the Council, in charge of presenting the report to the General Assembly, to report to Council members on relevant suggestions and observations raised during the debate. It is important that the Council convene soon after the General Assembly debate to reflect on these suggestions and observations.

We also call on all Council Presidents to submit their monthly assessments pursuant to paragraph 155 of presidential note 507, as these provide an important flow of information from the Council to the General Assembly. We note that, in 2024, just eight out of 12 Council Presidents submitted their monthly assessments. There should be more consistent and coordinated efforts from the Council in this regard. We hope that there will be progress on this particular issue because this is an issue that my delegation has raised repeatedly, both here and in the General Assembly.

Thirdly, my final point is about effectiveness. The Council’s record on this remains mixed, with swift decisions being taken on some issues but a lack of adequate action on other issues. For example, the delay in the appointment of the Chairs of subsidiary bodies until June this year was a severe setback to the implementation of Council decisions. We call on Council members to adhere to the guidelines for the selection of Chairs of subsidiary bodies contained in presidential note 507 and to avoid politicization of this process. More significantly, the indiscriminate use of the veto has continued to affect the Council, preventing it from acting in a timely and appropriate manner. It is especially disheartening to note that since the veto initiative resolution was adopted by the General Assembly in April 2022 (resolution 76/262), there have been 17 vetoes.

The permanent five have special privileges, and these must accordingly be wielded with special responsibility and special care. Our view is that the updated note on the Council’s working methods should clearly articulate the United Nations membership’s expectation for Council members to act in unity to discharge their responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. We believe that Council members, in particular the permanent members, should abstain from voting if they are party to a dispute, in line with Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter of the United Nations. Singapore also supports the French-Mexican initiative and the code of conduct of the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency Group on limiting the use of the veto in relation to mass atrocities (see S/2015/978).

Allow me to conclude by thanking the co-Chairs for their continued efforts on this issue. At a time when we are seeking to reform the United Nations system to make it more effective and fit for purpose, it behoves the Council to undertake practical reforms to the same end. We call on all Council members, in particular the permanent members, to engage constructively in this initiative to improve the working methods of the Council.

sources.title: Ms. Lassen (Denmark), speaking on behalf of the Nordic and Baltic States; Denmark: European States; Invited non-members of the Security Council; European Union member States; NATO members; High-income economy (World Bank, that year) — Security Council, 9410th meeting, 5 September 2023 — S/PV.9410 — Implementation of the note by the President of the Security Council (S/2017/507) Working methods of the Security Council

sources.text:
I have the honour to speak on behalf of the Nordic and Baltic States — Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden and my own country, Denmark.

I would first like to commend Albania for convening this annual debate and for its efforts as Chair of the Informal Working Group on Documentation and other Procedural Questions. As the past year has shown, it is vital for the Security Council to engage with all Member States on how to deliver on its mandate and become more transparent, effective, and inclusive. The recent engagement with the co-Chairs of the intergovernmental negotiations process is a small step in that direction. It is the Council’s working methods, and their continuing innovation, that enable the Council to function. But we have also seen that they can be used to render it paralysed on the most important matters of international peace and security. With a view to improving the performance of the Council and strengthening its working methods at this juncture, the Nordic and Baltic States would like to highlight three priority areas that demand our collective attention.

First, opportunities for the wider membership to engage meaningfully in the work of the Council remain key to ensuring that the Council can draw on their perspectives, knowledge and capacity, in line with Article 24 of the Charter of the United Nations. In that regard, the Peacebuilding Commission can offer valuable advice and cross-cutting perspectives in support of the Council’s work. In addition to providing written advice, its Chairs should be invited to brief the Council whenever possible, and there is room for the Council to make better use of that advice. We also urge for a more inclusive approach on the acceptance of rule 37 requests. We welcome the presidencies’ regular interactive wrap-in and wrap-up sessions. We also welcome efforts to include more female briefers from civil society. Continued attention to ensuring their safe participation and the deeply concerning issue of reprisals is critical to that end.

Secondly, elected members continue to bring invaluable innovation to the Council. Their ability to participate meaningfully in the Council’s work is indispensable, and we commend Ireland and the United Arab Emirates for their recent publication of the Interactive Handbook of the Working Methods of the Council for its elected members. In that regard, we align ourselves with the important recommendations made by the Secretary-General to the Security Council in his New Agenda for Peace, particularly on the need to democratize its procedures. That includes more burden-sharing among all Council members in terms of penholderships, systematic consultations with countries affected by Council decisions, such as host and troop- and police-contributing countries, and promoting greater accountability for permanent members in their use of the veto.

Thirdly, with regard to the right of the veto, the Nordic and Baltic States are of the view that the use of the veto should come with transparency and accountability. Permanent members should refrain from using it in cases of mass atrocities, including the crime of aggression. By adopting the veto initiative through its resolution 76/262, the General Assembly introduced an important accountability mechanism. We would encourage the formal adoption of the special reports produced to ensure their appropriate reflection in the Council’s annual report. Going forward, we would also like to see the Council consistently implement Article 27, paragraph 3, in line with the Charter’s overall objectives, particularly Article 2, paragraph 4. We would also welcome a chapter dedicated to the veto in the Council’s annual report.

In conclusion, we encourage Council members to continue to innovate and engage through the Working Group to create a more transparent, inclusive, accountable and therefore more effective Council, and we want to see its working methods implemented consistently. We also hope that the recommendations made today by the broader United Nations membership will be taken into account in the Council’s future work through adapting and improving its working methods.

sources.title: Mr. Katz Pavlotzky (Uruguay) (spoke in Spanish); Uruguay: States of the Americas; Invited non-members of the Security Council; Group of 77 members; High-income economy (World Bank, that year) — Security Council, 9571st meeting (resumption 1), 14 March 2024 — S/PV.9571 (Resumption 1) — Implementation of the note by the President of the Security Council (S/2017/507) — English text is the UN's translation from Spanish

sources.heading: Security Council, 9571st meeting (resumption 1) — Implementation of the note by the President of the Security Council (S/2017/507)
sources.text:
My delegation greatly appreciates the initiative of the presidency of Japan to convene an open debate to consider this theme. We consider the working methods of the Security Council a central issue which must be improved in order to make the Council’s action more effective and make its functioning more democratic.

The delegation of Uruguay associates itself, first of all, with the statement made by the representative of Norway on behalf of the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency (ACT) group, of which we are a member. That allows us to be very brief in the statement we deliver in our national capacity. We will therefore limit ourselves to mentioning some points of particular importance that we believe should be improved. These do not necessarily imply the adoption of new rules. In some cases, they only require the correct application of existing rules or regulations.

In particular, we would like to refer to the statement of the representative of the ACT group with regard to the absence, in the note by the President S/2017/507, of mentions of the veto. In that sense — and even though it can be understood that it goes beyond the working methods — its inclusion is essential to ensure the transparency and effectiveness of the Council’s actions.

With reference to the aforementioned presidential note 507, we thank the delegation of Japan for the initiative of updating it. We support that action because we understand that it is a living document that requires revisions in order to keep it up to date and serve the purposes for which it was created.

Turning to the ACT group’s statement, we fully share the concern regarding the need to seek the full implementation of Article 27, paragraph 3, of the Charter of the United Nations, including the principle, applicable to all members, that any party to a dispute must abstain from participating and voting on that matter. We recall that this Article — like all other provisions — must be interpreted in a manner consistent with all the purposes and principles of the Charter.

The second key aspect is that all members of the Council, permanent and non-permanent, must commit to not vote against and to effectively support actions to prevent or stop mass atrocities. That commitment is part of the ACT code of conduct, which is in line with the Franco-Mexican initiative to limit the use of the veto in cases of mass human rights violations, which has very strong support among the membership of the Organization.

We understand that those suggestions generally respond to the three guiding questions outlined in the concept note (S/2024/208/Rev.1, annex), considering them essential, including those that should be implemented through a more effective application of existing norms or the adoption of complementary ones.

Another priority is the full, equitable and meaningful participation of women in the work of the Council. We therefore insist on the need to broadly integrate gender perspectives into the Council’s working methods.

We reiterate that the Security Council must strengthen its engagement with the entire membership of the United Nations, as well as its cooperation and interaction with the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, the Human Rights Council and other entities within the system, especially the Peacebuilding Commission.

We stress the importance of cooperation between the General Assembly and the Security Council. That is why we believe that the adoption and corresponding implementation of resolution General Assembly 76/262 is a top priority. It represents a major step forward in the coordination and mutual reinforcement of the work between the Security Council and the General Assembly. It also helps reach our objective and better regulate the implementation and use of the veto mechanism.

sources.title: Mr. Van Schalkwyk (South Africa); South Africa: African States; Invited non-members of the Security Council; African Union member States; Non-Aligned Movement members; Group of 77 members; Upper-middle-income economy (World Bank, that year) — Security Council, 10043rd meeting (resumption 1), 14 November 2025 — S/PV.10043 (Resumption 1) — Implementation of the note by the President of the Security Council (S/2024/507)

sources.text:
South Africa appreciates the opportunity to participate in this open debate on this important subject. I would also like to thank the briefers for their briefings. These are people who we know remain authoritative experts on the functioning of the work of the Security Council.

Addressing the structural challenges in the composition of the Council through Security Council reform remains paramount. However, improving its working methods may contribute to a more inclusive, efficient and transparent functioning of the Council that delivers better on its mandate in the interim. We express our appreciation for the significant work done by the elected members of the Security Council, led by Japan, to codify the working methods of the Council in its note by the President S/2017/507, the latest of which was adopted in December last year (S/2024/507).

In recent years, the Council’s functioning has improved, with a greater role played by the elected members of the Council. This includes a more active role for these members, based on their respective comparative expertise as penholders forresolutions and various outcomes of the Council. We appreciate that the African members of the Council have been afforded a greater role in this regard, especially in terms of matters affecting the African continent. We welcome the continued engagement between the Peace and Security Council of the African Union and the United Nations Security Council to further synergize efforts to bring about lasting peace through the permanent silencing of the guns in Africa. In this regard, we look forward to the twelfth high-level seminar on peace and security in Africa, or the Oran Process, taking place in Algeria in December this year. The Government of Algeria is commended for its sustained efforts in facilitating this discussion.

We have also witnessed stronger mechanisms to ensure the accountability of the Security Council to the broader United Nations membership, especially in terms of its lack of action when needed most, such as in the case of Gaza. The adoption of General Assembly resolution 76/262, holding permanent members accountable for the use of the veto, has assisted in this regard. South Africa has supported further restraints on the use of the veto by supporting the French and Mexican initiative on the non-use of the veto in cases of mass atrocities. However, this cannot replace the need for urgent Council reform to redress the challenges brought about by the use of the veto for narrow self-interests by some States.

While we welcome the improvements with regard to the Council’s process on the selection and appointment of the Secretary-General, such as the issuing of joint letters from the Presidents of the Council and the General Assembly, more transparency is also encouraged in the process within the Council on the selection of the Secretary-General, as this is a matter of interest to all Member States. Ultimately, we recall that according to Article 97 of the Charter of the United Nations, it is the General Assembly that appoints the Secretary-General, upon the recommendation of the Council. Therefore, the Council must do more to ensure that its recommendation processes are transparent and allow the General Assembly to exercise its authority on this matter.

Finally, South Africa would also like to encourage the Council to determine, in advance of establishing new peacekeeping mandates, the sources of funding of such mandates in view of the current liquidity crisis, as well as other resources that may be required particularly for peace agreements established through political processes, in which the Council or United Nations was not involved, or the re-hatting or transitioning of peacekeeping missions.

sources.text:
The delegation of the Republic of Paraguay appreciates the opportunity to speak in this debate and congratulates Sierra Leone on its assumption of the presidency of the Security Council. We understand that the annual debates on the working methods of the Security Council are a moment of singular importance for the evolution of an efficient, effective elected body capable of honoring the mandate conferred upon it by the Charter of the United Nations. We also thank the briefers for their briefings.

The responsibility of achieving and maintaining international peace and security is the fundamental purpose of the Council. It must also facilitate the three pillars of the work of the United Nations.

Although they may seem minor issues, the predictability in the appointment of the Chairs and Vice-Chairs of subsidiary bodies, the rotating presidency with guarantees in place to ensure that non-permanent members can exercise that function at least once during their membership, and transparency in the negotiation processes leading to resolutions, presidential statements and notes affecting the rules of procedure are issues of great importance given the Council’s influence within the United Nations .

The relationship between the General Assembly and the Security Council remains a matter of paramount importance. Our delegation believes that this relationship must be strengthened and that the Council must recognize that its legitimacy depends on the respect of the entire membership and the faithful fulfillment of its mandate. It must therefore make efforts to become more representative, inclusive, transparent, effective and accountable for its decisions.

The security pillar is under scrutiny by the international community. Undoubtedly, even though it is not a universally representative body, the work of the Security Council is largely the global barometer of the United Nations performance in ensuring the maintenance of international peace and security. In that regard, we welcome the efforts of the Informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions to publish its annual report, guided by the principles of openness, dialogue and inclusion. That must continue.

Paraguay believes that public meetings should be the norm and not the exception. We understand the sensitivity of the issues dealt with by the Council, and therefore, in exceptional situations, closed or private meetings should be allowed, always with the knowledge of the membership at large. We believe that, for negotiations on specific situations such as the first drafts of resolutions, bilateral and multilateral channels can be used and that, when the draft resolutions are in blue, they should be distributed to the full membership.

Member States have witnessed significant differences of opinion regarding the use of the veto, especially during recent sessions of the intergovernmental negotiations on the reform of this organ. Paraguay believes that the veto should be abolished, limited or formally restricted, especially in cases involving measures to prevent the most serious crimes or mass atrocities.

It is also vitally important to recognize that the use of this prerogative must be commensurate with the great responsibility it entails. It must therefore be used with complete transparency and prudence and entails a duty of accountability, in accordance with the principle of the sovereign equality of States under Article 2, paragraph 1, of the Charter. In the same vein, we believe that the members of the United Nations cannot comply with the Charter selectively, and we therefore urge full compliance with Article 27, paragraph 3.

Lasty, Paraguay is of the view that the possibility of allowing States parties that are not members of the Security Council to serve as Chair or Vice-Chair of subsidiary bodies of the Council should be considered when the nature of the forum so permits.

sources.title: Mrs. González López (El Salvador) (spoke in Spanish); El Salvador: States of the Americas; Invited non-members of the Security Council; Group of 77 members; Upper-middle-income economy (World Bank, that year) — Security Council, 10210th meeting (resumption 1), 19 August 2026 — S/PV.10210 (Resumption 1) — Implementation of the note by the President of the Security Council (S/2024/507) — English text is the UN's translation from Spanish

sources.heading: Security Council, 10210th meeting (resumption 1) — Implementation of the note by the President of the Security Council (S/2024/507)
sources.text:
El Salvador thanks you, Mr. President, for convening this debate and for your efforts to continue promoting an open discussion on the working methods of the Security Council.

We reaffirm the positions expressed by our delegation in previous debates on the need for a more transparent, inclusive, representative and effective Council. Today we would like to focus on some areas where we believe concrete progress is needed.

First, we wish to highlight the relationship between the Security Council and the Peacebuilding Commission. El Salvador has consistently advocated strengthening the complementarity between the two bodies and, as a current member of the Commission, reaffirms its commitment to playing an active role in deepening this relationship. The Commission can provide the Council with a preventive and long-term perspective, based on national ownership and a broader understanding of the factors that sustain peace. However, the Commission’s contribution must come early enough to influence decisions if it is to have an impact. We therefore encourage the Council and those responsible f or drafting to seek the Commission’s advice more systematically, in particular before mandate renewals and transitions, and to make more specific requests for timely and relevant recommendations from the Commission. The note by the President of the Security Council (S/2024/507) already provides tools, including informal interactive dialogues with the Chair of the Commission and country-specific configurations.

Secondly, it is impossible to separate working methods from the effects of the veto. El Salvador reiterates its deep concern about the use of the veto and the continuing consequences for the Council’s ability to act in response to threats to international peace and security. This concern is not limited to the formal veto. The explicit or implicit threat of using the veto can also prevent proposals from being put forward, negotiated or put to a vote. In other words, Council paralysis is not always reflected in the voting record. We therefore support continuing to explore measures to limit the use of the veto, increase transparency regarding its effects and strengthen existing accountability mechanisms. In that regard, we reaffirm our support for General Assembly resolution 76/262 and for the role of the General Assembly when the Council fails to act. We believe that accountability must encompass not only the decisions that the Council takes but also those that it fails to take.

Thirdly, we want to refer to the function of penholdership and co -penholdership. The 10 elected members represent two thirds of the Council’s membership and bring regional perspectives, experience and political capacity that must find substantive expression in the preparation of its decisions. We value the gradual expansion of co - penholdership among permanent and elected members. Such arrangements can combine institutional memory with regional knowledge and help to enhance the legitimacy and support of the Council’s products. However, co-penholdership must go further. It requires real responsibilities, timely consultations, sufficient time to negotiate and a genuine search for consensus. This responsibility also includes listening to those who will have to implement the decisions adopted. In particular, before renewing or modifying mandates of peace operations, penholders and co-penholders must hold substantive and timely consultations with troop- and police-contributing countries, and their views must be duly taken into account when drafting texts. These consultations cannot become a formality. They must enable the Council’s decisions to reflect the operational realities on the ground.

Fourthly, the ongoing process for the selection and appointment of the next Secretary-General is concrete evidence of the transparency and inclusiveness that we seek to strengthen. We appreciate the progress made in membership participation and consider it essential to preserve it during all stages of the process. Transparency should not diminish as the process moves towards the Council. There should be close and continuous coordination with the General Assembly, predictable rules and equitable access to relevant information for all Member States. The Organization’s next leadership must emerge from a process that strengthens, not diminishes, the membership’s trust in the United Nations.

Lastly, we reiterate that women’s full, equal and meaningful participation must remain an integral part of the Council’s working methods. This requires not only ensuring their participation as briefers but also systematically incorporating the analysis of the differentiated impact of conflicts on women and girls into the Council’s deliberations and decisions.

Working methods are not merely a procedural matter. They determine who is involved, who can influence a decision, what perspectives are heard and ultimately the Council’s ability to act. El Salvador will continue to contribute to this effort in the conviction that a Council that is more inclusive in its processes will also be a Council that is more legitimate and more effective in its decisions.

sources.title: Mr. Pipia (Georgia); Georgia: Asian States; Invited non-members of the Security Council; Upper-middle-income economy (World Bank, that year) — Security Council, 9962nd meeting (resumption 2), 24 July 2025 — S/PV.9962 (Resumption 2) — Maintenance of international peace and security

sources.heading: Security Council, 9962nd meeting (resumption 2) — Maintenance of international peace and security
sources.text:
At the outset, let me express our gratitude to the presidency of Pakistan for convening this important debate.

Georgia aligns itself with the statement made on behalf of the European Union, and I would like to make some additional remarks in my national capacity.

Multilateralism and a global, rules-based international system with the United Nations at its core are key to ensuring the maintenance of international peace and security. However, today we are seeing multilateralism undergo one of the most challenging periods since the establishment of the United Nations. Nearly eight decades since the Organization was founded, we still live in a world in which the founding principles of the United Nations are violated on a daily basis, as conflicts rage all over the world. Moreover, grave threats stemming from hybrid warfare, pandemic diseases, technology-enabled cyberrelated threats and the rapid spread of disinformation, coupled with unmitigated climate change, exacerbate this gloomy reality. Unfortunately, my own country is no exception.

As I speak, Russia’s illegal occupation of two regions of my country — the Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions — persists, in blatant violation of the fundamental principles and norms of international law, the Charter of the United Nations and Russia’s other international commitments, inter alia, the European Union-mediated ceasefire agreement of 12 August 2008. Russia’s illegal occupation of the Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions of Georgia continues to have severe impacts on the population of those regions and the areas adjacent to the occupation line. Both regions remain heavily militarized, with the presence of Russia’s full-fledged military bases. Russia’s ongoing steps towards the de facto annexation of these Georgian regions by gradually dragging them into its military, political, economic social and legal systems further aggravate the situation. Let me also underline that, to this very day, even international human rights mechanisms are not allowed to enter the occupied regions.

We believe that multilateralism and respect for the rules-based international order must serve as the foundation for eliminating these threats, ensuring international peace and security, upholding human rights and attaining sustainable development. However, multilateralism works when the members of the international community abide by common rules and principles. While governments have the primary responsibility for peacebuilding and sustaining peace, the United Nations system can also do more to build more peaceful and resilient societies.

In this context, within reform of the broader United Nations system, Security Council reform has a special role to play. That is also reflected in the recently adopted Pact for the Future (General Assembly resolution 79/1), which states that Security Council reform should be a Member States-driven process. Our position implies equitable representation and enlargement of the Security Council and reform of the use of the veto, the working methods and the decision-making principles of the Council, in addition to greater accountability before the General Assembly, as those elements will increase the Council’s legitimacy, authority and credibility. In line with the United Nations Charter, no State shall take precedence over another State or be above the authority of the collective decisions made by the United Nations. Without going into details, let me underline the need for the Council to fully enforce the current United Nations Charter, in particular Article 27, paragraph 3, which stipulates that in a series of specific, important decisions, a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. Moreover, the restriction of the right of the veto shall be applied when the Security Council addresses core crimes.

Furthermore, coordination between the United Nations and regional organizations can also play an important role in conflict prevention and post-conflict recovery, reconstruction and development, as those organizations are better equipped to deal with the peculiar challenges informed by regional and subregional contexts. The United Nations should continue endeavours aimed at addressing pressing global challenges through collective actions. We shall collectively recommit to ensuring a peaceful world based on international law, with the United Nations Charter at its core, better upholding human rights and implementing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

In conclusion, let me underscore that our collective promise of peace, security, human rights and sustainable development depends entirely on our commitment to the United Nations Charter and international law.

sources.title: Mr. Abd Karim (Malaysia); Malaysia: Asian States; Invited non-members of the Security Council; Organisation of Islamic Cooperation member States; Non-Aligned Movement members; Group of 77 members; Upper-middle-income economy (World Bank, that year) — Security Council, 9861st meeting (resumption 2), 20 February 2025 — S/PV.9861 (Resumption 2) — Maintenance of international peace and security
sources.agenda: Maintenance of international peace and security
sources.heading: Security Council, 9861st meeting (resumption 2) — Maintenance of international peace and security
sources.text:
Malaysia wishes you success, Sir, during China’s presidency of the Security Council. We thank the Secretary-General for his insightful briefing on 18 February.

The United Nations is the seat of multilateralism. It is where Member States cooperate based on common interests and mutual respect for the sovereignty of all, big and small. The United Nations is where States confer to form consensus on the rules that should govern our relations. It is a place where we foster shared responsibility to maintain an order that is based on rules rather than the “might makes right” principle so as to ensure a peaceful, stable and prosperous world.

Sadly, at times, reality paints a different picture. The rules we make have failed to protect the innocent from heinous crimes. For example, the United Nations has been unable to stop the maiming and killing of women and children in Gaza. Even when the overwhelming majority of Member States have demanded an end to these atrocities, it was overruled in this very Chamber. The maiming and killing continue with impunity. Gaza is but one tragedy. The United Nations seems equally powerless to stop the suffering in Myanmar, the Sudan and Ukraine. We must confront reality. This inability to act decisively exposes deep flaws within the system that hinder effective intervention and sustainable solutions.

Reform of the Security Council is imperative. Malaysia is unequivocal in its conviction that the veto power must be abolished in the long run. Until that is achieved, the veto must be completely prohibited in cases of mass atrocity crimes such as genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes. In addition, we believe that to be effective, the veto should be exercised by at least two permanent members and supported by three non-permanent members of the Security Council. The decision should then be endorsed by the General Assembly through a simple majority vote.

We must uphold multilateralism under the United Nations. It is the only system that provides protection for all, both big and small. It is truly the most representative world organization and is therefore unsurpassed in its legitimacy. Undoubtedly, this system is not without its flaws. It can and must be improved, but it should never be bypassed.

I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of a group of 61 Member States: Albania, Australia, Austria, Bahrain, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Cabo Verde, Canada, Costa Rica, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, the Dominican Republic, Djibouti, Ecuador, El Salvador, Estonia, Fiji, Finland, Georgia, Germany, Guatemala, Jamaica, Jordan, Kuwait, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Liberia, Libya, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Maldives, Malta, the Marshall Islands, Mexico, Monaco, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Norway, Palau, Poland, Portugal, the Republic of Moldova, Romania, Timor-Leste, Türkiye, Samoa, San Marino, Singapore, Slovakia, Spain, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Sweden, Switzerland, Qatar, Ukraine and my own country, New Zealand.

We welcome today’s open debate as a timely opportunity to consider the central tenets of the United Nations as embodied in its Charter — effective multilateralism, the maintenance of international law and the rule of law. As my Austrian colleague said, founded in the ashes of the Second World War, the United Nations is, fundamentally, an international peace and security organization, and it is the Council that has the primary responsibility in that regard. Yet we are faced with a reality in which the Council is increasingly unable to live up to that responsibility. Major crises and conflicts are too often met by inaction and paralysis.

We have also continued to witness with alarming frequency the use of the veto, whereby the Council is prevented from taking effective action in line with its mandate. The application of the veto — not to mention those draft resolutions discarded owing to the threat of a veto — undermines multilateral approaches. That favours contestation over cooperation on matters of international peace and security. Its effect is one of disillusionment and mistrust.

We as a group remain committed to finding ways to contemporize our multilateral institutions, despite their imperfections, so that they are best positioned to respond to the collective challenges we face, particularly as they relate to international peace and security.

We are pleased that the Pact for the Future (General Assembly resolution 79/1) contains many elements that, when implemented, will better enable the Council to deliver on its mandate, a mandate that requires the Council to act on behalf of all of us. We have all agreed on the urgency of further and meaningful Security Council reform.

The Pact calls for the full implementation of the Charter of the United Nations, highlighting Article 27, paragraph 3, which obliges parties to a dispute to abstain from voting on relevant Chapter VI resolutions. If any lack of clarity on the scope or definition of that clause is the reason that Charter obligation has not been honoured in full, it must be addressed as a matter of priority. Importantly, the Pact also includes language that aims to strengthen the relationship between the Council and the General Assembly. The General Assembly, where all 193 States Members of the United Nations are represented, is the very embodiment of multilateralism. Under the Charter, the Security Council is afforded primary but not exclusive responsibility for international peace and security. Chapter IV makes it clear that the General Assembly, too, has a role and responsibility in that regard. The Pact is explicit about the ability of the Assembly to take action. General Assembly resolutions 377 (V) and 76/262, on the emergency special session and the veto initiative respectively, established important platforms for action in the General Assembly.

The Pact also requires us to revitalize the General Assembly while we work in tandem to reform the Council. Our goal must be to ensure that the United Nations as a whole is able to act on matters of international peace and security, fulfil the mandate that we gave it by signing the Charter and deliver for the people whom we serve. The Council and the Assembly must work more closely, as envisaged in the Charter, and in the spirit of multilateralism. The General Assembly must strengthen its role in peace and security when the Council cannot act. The recently published Assembly for Peace handbook, commissioned by the President of the General Assembly, outlines the breadth of precedent that the General Assembly can draw from in that respect. The Council, in turn, should increasingly recognize General Assembly action on matters of international peace and security and draw inspiration from Assembly products and actions in formulating Council resolutions and products.

Finally, delivering on our collective commitment to multilateralism and to the international rule of law hinges on implementation of the commitments made at the United Nations .

sources.text:
I have the honour to address the Council on behalf of the Nordic countries: Denmark, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and my own country, Finland.

I thank Denmark and Pakistan for this timely debate and Security Council Report for the briefing.

The way in which the Security Council operates and takes decisions is a legitimate concern for the entire United Nations membership, as the Council, in line with Article 24 of the Charter of the United Nations, acts on their behalf. We all have a vested interest in ensuring the Council can properly and more efficiently respond to today’s many challenges.

The selection and appointment of the next Secretary-General is one of the most significant decisions at hand. The interactive dialogues with the candidates in the General Assembly, including engagement with civil society, have been instrumental in advancing the key principles of transparency and inclusivity and should remain an integral part of the process. We encourage the Council to uphold the same high standards in its own deliberations. This includes ensuring an equal and fair procedure for all candidates.

The selection and appointment process is a joint endeavour of the General Assembly and the Security Council, and the results of the Council’s straw polls should be communicated to the Member States of the General Assembly in an appropriate manner rather than through inevitable leaks. We further underscore the importance of geographical balance and gender equality and are encouraged by the number of highly qualified women candidates.

The Nordic countries remain deeply concerned by the continued inability of the Council to reach agreement on the allocation of the Chairs and the Vice -Chairs of the subsidiary bodies. The uncertainty may have consequences extending beyond the current Council term. This is not merely a procedural matter. We share the concern expressed by the elected members in their letter in July that this prolonged impasse undermines the credibility, effectiveness and institutional integrity of the Council and hampers its ability to discharge its Charter responsibilities. We call on those Council members who are currently preventing consensus to demonstrate flexibility to finally resolve this issue. Looking ahead, we believe that efforts should be made to review and improve the process, including in the context of the Informal Working Group.

The Nordic countries continue to support a more equitable distribution of work within the Security Council. While progress has been made through co -penholdership and more equal participation by elected members, penholdership still remains largely the responsibility of a limited number of Council members. Broader participation would better reflect the diverse perspectives in the Council and make fuller use of the regional expertise and insights of all elected members.

Working methods must continue to evolve. We therefore encourage the Council to regularly review and update note by the President S/2024/507 to ensure that it remains relevant. Continued and determined efforts are needed to strengthen the Council’s transparency, accountability and effectiveness. One such mechanism is the veto initiative, whereby the General Assembly is convened after a veto is cast. It is imperative to make the Council more accountable to the wider United Nations membership, whose trust and confidence are essential to the Council’s legitimacy.
